newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Jakarta stocks slip on money market liquidity fear.
newsitem.headline: Jakarta stocks slip on money market liquidity fear.

text.p: Jakarta stocks ended weaker on Friday, failing to be cheered by the Indonesian central bank's move to ease liquidity in the money market, brokers and analysts said.

Thursday's steep fall of 3.13 percent in the composite index looked to be partially erased in morning trade after the central Bank Indonesia announced it was cutting rates on its short-term certificates (SBIs) with maturities of one week and above by 50 basis points.
But the bank maintained high rates for shorter-term papers.
The index ended down 2.50 points, or 0.37 percent, at 675.44 as fears of a liquidity squeeze continued to rule, brokers said. The index was down 6.42 percent from 721.77 last Friday.
"It briefly boosted sentiment, but the market lost momentum later as worries over a liquidity squeeze haunted the market again," Goei Sauw Hong, an analyst with SocGen-Crosby Securities, said.
The bank cut rates on seven-day bilateral SBIs to 9.5 percent from 10.0 percent, but it maintained rates on high overnight bilateral SBIs at 14.0 percent and four-to-six day paper at 15.0 percent.
SBIs are short-term rupiah denominated obligations issued by the central bank to drain liquidity from the market.
"It (the market) is likely to remain weak...as the overnight rates are still high," Robert Allison, head of sales with Paribas Asia Equity, said.
Bank Indonesia had earlier increased the SBI short-term rates to reduce speculative attacks on the rupiah.
The policy, however, had tightened rupiah liquidity, pushed up the rupiah interbank rate and prompted banks to increase interest rates, the analysts said.
They said sentiment was likely to remain weak in the short-term as the sharp falls were due to the accumulation of worries over several factors, with high overnight rates as the main reason.

Worries over new margin finance regulations and rights issue payments were likely to keep sentiment weak in the near term, William Keeling, head of research with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Research in Jakarta, said in a report.

Keeling said some 6.74 trillion rupiah in rights issue payments were in the offing over the next four weeks. This is an unprecedented amount of fund-raising by existing companies and is equivalent to 2.6 percent of the Jakarta Stock Exchange's market capitalisation of 260 trillion rupiah ($100 billion).
This excluded cash demands made by new initial public offerings, Keeling said.
Analysts and brokers said the new margin finance regulations which limit domestic retail client leverage also hurt sentiment.
"The introduction of margin finance regulations may, if immediately and strictly enforced, cause disruption," Keeling said.
A growing proportion of retail investors are operating on margin finance.

The typical margin investor is probably 300 percent geared on the underlying cash deposit held the stockbroking company. If the client is fully invested and is faced by a rights issue, the only options are to increase leverage or sell stock, Keeling said.
